topic.title: Configuring DITA Specializations for Translation
topic.shortdesc: How to make the translation agent aware of custom DITA specializations.

body.p: The agent recognizes any well-formed XML file as translatable content, so a topic written in a custom DITA specialization is picked up for translation without any configuration. What you need to configure separately is how it is validated and how it is translated.

section.title: Configuring Validation Rules
section.p: Validation decides which elements and attributes must be left untouched and which must be translated. You can extend or override the built-in rules for a specialization by adding an optional .contentfusion/i18n/validation-rules.xml file to your workspace:
The rules that apply to a document come from three layers, in order of increasing precedence:

ol.li: Built-in defaults - The rules the agent always starts from (described below). They apply even when no validation-rules.xml file exists.
<global> rules - Your project-wide additions and overrides, applied to every document.

<match root="…"> rules - Overrides for documents whose root element matches the given name, which is how you target one specialization without affecting others. They win over both <global> and the defaults for documents with that root.

section.p: You rarely need to list every element and attribute, because each kind has a sensible default:

ul.li: Elements default to translatable. An element's text is translated unless a built-in rule or your own <keep-unchanged> entry explicitly protects it. Listing an element under <translate> is only useful to override a protection that would otherwise apply.

Attributes default to protected. An attribute is left unchanged unless a built-in rule or your own <translate> entry explicitly allows it to be translated. This is why a custom specialization usually only needs <translate> entries for its own label-like attributes, and rarely needs <keep-unchanged> for attributes.

section.p: In short: for elements, list the exceptions that must not be translated; for attributes, list the exceptions that must be translated.

The built-in defaults already protect the usual non-translatable DITA content (code, identifiers, keys, and similar) and already allow translation of the standard text-bearing attributes (such as navtitle, alt, spectitle, reftitle, standby, and value). Add rules only for the elements or attributes specific to your specialization that these defaults do not already handle correctly.

section.title: Describing a Specialization in agent-instructions.md
section.p: Validation rules only constrain the output; they do not teach the agent about your specialization's semantics. Write a short Markdown file that describes it in plain language (for example learning-content-guide.md) and reference it from agent-instructions.md. The agent applies this guidance, together with its general DITA knowledge, when translating documents that use your specialization.
Based on how the built-in doctype guidance is written, cover the following when you describe your own specialization:

ul.li: Titles and labels vs. body content - Which elements are titles, headings, or UI labels (which should read tersely, like a heading) versus narrative prose, including any titles nested inside structural children.
Protected, technical-looking content - Elements or attributes that look like ordinary words but are really identifiers, keys, or code and must stay exactly as written.
Context-dependent elements - Elements that are only translatable in some contexts and act as fixed tokens in others.

Which attributes may change - Call out the specific attributes on your specialization's elements that hold translatable text (labels, alt text, and similar), since attributes are protected by default.
Tricky examples - For any case that is easy to get wrong, include a short before/after example showing the source and its expected translation.
